Central Nervous System
Histology
Ear

Quick Overview

The ear serves equilibrium and hearing and is divided into the external, middle and inner ear. This lesson covers the histology of each part: the auricle, meatus and tympanic membrane, the air-filled middle ear with its ossicles and auditory tube, and the fluid-filled inner ear. The inner ear section focuses on the bony and membranous labyrinths, the vestibular receptors (maculae and cristae ampullares) and the cochlear duct with the organ of Corti.

Complete Lesson Content

Divisions of the ear

The functions of the ear relate to equilibrium and hearing. It consists of three parts: the external ear, the middle ear and the inner ear.

I. External ear

1. Auricle (pinna)

An irregularly shaped plate of elastic cartilage covered on all sides by tightly adherent thin skin.

2. External auditory meatus

  • A canal extending from the auricle to the tympanic membrane.
  • Outer third: elastic cartilage. Inner two-thirds: bony (temporal bone).
  • Lined by skin with numerous hairs and sebaceous glands.
  • Contains ceruminous glands (modified sweat glands) that secrete cerumen, a waxy material forming a sticky barrier against foreign bodies.

3. Tympanic membrane (eardrum)

Separates the external ear from the middle ear. It has three layers:

  • Outer surface: very thin skin.
  • Middle layer: tough connective tissue of collagen, elastic fibers and fibroblasts arranged in circular and radial patterns.
  • Inner surface: simple cuboidal epithelium.

II. Middle ear

  • A box-like air space inside the temporal bone.
  • Lined by mucous membrane: simple squamous epithelium resting on lamina propria.
  • Contains three small auditory ossicles, the malleus, incus and stapes, connected by small muscles (stapedius and tensor tympani).
  • Windows: the medial wall has two membrane-covered openings, the oval window and the round window.

Auditory (Eustachian) tube

  • Connects the middle ear cavity with the nasopharynx.
  • Posterior one-third is bony; anterior two-thirds is elastic cartilage.
  • Epithelium varies: ciliated columnar posteriorly near the middle ear cavity, and pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells near the pharynx.
  • Usually collapsed, but opens during swallowing to balance air pressure.

III. Inner ear

Composed of two labyrinths, bony and membranous.

Bony labyrinth

A system of cavities and canals in the petrous part of the temporal bone, filled with perilymph. It consists of the cochlea, vestibule and semicircular canals.

  • Cochlea: its cavity is divided into three spaces by two membranes (basilar and vestibular). The scala vestibuli (above) and scala tympani (below) contain perilymph; the scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph.
  • Vestibule: located anterior to the semicircular canals and posterior to the cochlea; houses the utricle and saccule.
  • Semicircular canals: three (anterior, posterior, lateral), arranged at right angles to each other. All arise from and return to the vestibule, and each has a dilatation, the ampulla, at one end.

Membranous labyrinth

  • Housed within the bony labyrinth; formed of membranous sacs and ducts and filled with endolymph.
  • It floats in perilymph, and the two fluids are separated by the membranous labyrinth.
  • Walls are thin connective tissue sheaths lined by simple squamous epithelium, except in certain areas covered by specialized neuroepithelial cells that act as receptors for vestibular and auditory stimuli.
  • Three semicircular ducts arise from the utricle.

The inner ear has two sensory organs that differ functionally and morphologically: the vestibular apparatus (equilibrium) and the auditory apparatus (hearing).

Utricle and saccule (maculae)

Two communicating sacs of the membranous labyrinth housed in the vestibule. Their walls contain receptor areas called the maculae (macula utriculi and macula sacculi). Each macula contains receptor cells (hair cells) and supporting cells.

Cell typeFeatures
Type I hair cellFlask-shaped; rigid stereocilia and a single true cilium (kinocilium), which is immotile.
Type II hair cellSimilar structure to type I but columnar in shape.
Supporting cellColumnar, resting on the basement membrane; produces the thick gelatinous glycoprotein mass (otolithic membrane) covering the receptor cells.
  • The basal parts of both hair cell types are surrounded by cup-shaped afferent nerve endings.
  • The surface of the otolithic membrane contains numerous calcium carbonate crystals called otoliths.

Semicircular ducts (cristae ampullares)

The semicircular ducts occupy and have the same shape as the semicircular canals. Their receptor areas are the cristae ampullares.

The crista is structurally similar to the macula, but its glycoprotein layer is thicker, has a conical form called the cupula, and is not covered by otoliths.

Cochlear duct and organ of Corti

The cochlear duct is the scala media of the cochlea. Its covering epithelium varies by location:

  • Over the vestibular membrane: squamous.
  • Laterally: low columnar epithelium over capillary-rich connective tissue, called the stria vascularis, the site of endolymph secretion.
  • Its sensory area is the organ of Corti, composed of supporting cells and hair cells.

Supporting cells

These rest on the basilar membrane, which forms the floor of the cochlear duct.

CellFeatures
Inner and outer pillar cellsTall cells with a wide base and narrow apex; outline the tunnel of Corti.
Inner and outer phalangeal cellsColumnar cells on the basilar membrane. Inner cells form a single row surrounding the inner hair cells; outer cells support the three or four rows of outer hair cells.
Border cellsColumnar; support the inner border of the organ of Corti.
Cells of HensenElongated, polygonal; support the outer border of the organ of Corti.

Hair cells

  • Columnar cells that do not rest on the basilar membrane; they occupy a cup-shaped recess on the upper surface of the phalangeal cells.
  • Apical surfaces carry stereocilia (no kinocilium), embedded in the tectorial membrane, a rigid gelatinous glycoprotein-rich membrane.
  • Their bases have afferent and efferent nerve endings.
  • Inner hair cells: a single row on the inner phalangeal cells, lining the inner margin of the tunnel.
  • Outer hair cells: three or four rows supported by the outer phalangeal cells, lining the outer margin of the tunnel.

Key Points / Quick Review

External ear

  • Auricle: elastic cartilage plate with thin adherent skin.
  • Meatus: outer third cartilage, inner two-thirds bone; hairs, sebaceous and ceruminous glands (cerumen).
  • Tympanic membrane: thin skin / collagen-elastic layer (circular and radial) / simple cuboidal epithelium.

Middle ear

  • Air-filled; simple squamous lining on lamina propria.
  • Malleus, incus, stapes; stapedius and tensor tympani; oval and round windows.
  • Auditory tube: posterior third bony, anterior two-thirds elastic cartilage; opens in swallowing.

Labyrinths and fluids

  • Bony labyrinth (cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals): perilymph.
  • Membranous labyrinth: endolymph, floating in perilymph.
  • Scala vestibuli and tympani: perilymph; scala media: endolymph.

Vestibular receptors

  • Maculae (utricle, saccule): type I and II hair cells, supporting cells, otolithic membrane with otoliths.
  • Cristae ampullares (semicircular ducts): thicker conical cupula, no otoliths.

Cochlear duct

  • Stria vascularis (lateral wall) secretes endolymph.
  • Organ of Corti: pillar, phalangeal, border and Hensen cells on the basilar membrane.

Organ of Corti hair cells

  • Sit in recesses of phalangeal cells; stereocilia only, embedded in the tectorial membrane.
  • Inner: one row; outer: three or four rows.
